sections.history: Tirukkurukavur, a quiet village a few kilometres from Sirkazhi, is sung in the Tevaram as Tirukkurukavur Velladai by both Sambandar and Sundarar, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam, counted as the thirteenth such shrine on the northern bank of the Kaveri. Tradition places an early Chola temple here by the seventh century, the age of the hymns. Inscriptions from the reigns of Rajendra Chola, Kulottunga Chola I and Vikrama Chola show that worship continued through the great Chola centuries, and the stone temple that stands today is held to have been raised in the late tenth century under Uttama Chola. The place has carried several old names, among them Rishabhapuram and Vishnupuram, each recalling a story told of this shrine.
sections.architecture: This is a small village temple in the Chola manner, built of stone around a single sanctum in which Shiva is worshipped as Velvidai Nathar, also called Velladai Nathar, the Lord of the White Bull. The goddess Kaviyankanni, also known as Neelotpala Visalakshi, has her own shrine facing south. Shrines to Ganesha, Durga and Murugan with his consorts Valli and Deivanai stand within the enclosure. The sacred tree is the bilva. Before the temple lies a tank and, within the precincts, the well called Paal Kinaru, the milk well, the most singular feature of the place. The temple was last consecrated in 1986.
sections.legends: Three stories are told here. In the first, Vishnu took the form of a white bull, a vellai edabam, and worshipped Shiva in this place, hence the name Velvidai and the old names Rishabhapuram and Vishnupuram. In the second, the young Sambandar, travelling weary and hungry, was received by an old man who gave him and his companions curd rice and a place to rest; when the saint woke, the house and its host were gone, and he understood the Lord himself had fed him. From this the place was once called Dadyonnapuram, the town of curd rice. In the third, Sambandar, wishing to bathe at Kashi to cleanse himself of the harm his debates had brought, was directed here, where Shiva is said to have brought the Ganga into the well. Sundarar is also said to have sung his hymn after the Lord's grace here.
sections.festivals: On the new moon of the Tamil month of Thai, in January or February, the water of the milk well is said to turn white, and the well, kept closed for the rest of the year, is opened for bathing; the image of Sambandar is brought in procession from the temple at Sirkazhi for the Theerthavari rite. On the full moon of Chithirai, in April or May, curd rice is offered to all who come, in memory of the old man's meal, and devotees believe that prayer here keeps a household free from want of food. Thai Poosam, Skanda Sashti, Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are also observed. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tirukkurukavur is a place for a slow visit by those who enjoy small village shrines. The temple lies about a kilometre from the main road, among fields, and is usually very quiet. Come first to the sanctum of Velvidai Nathar, then to the south-facing shrine of Kaviyankanni, and ask the priests about the milk well and the old man with the curd rice. Many pilgrims time their visit for the Chithirai full moon, when the meal of curd rice is shared again as it was in Sambandar's story. Combine the visit with nearby Paadal Petra temples such as Tirumullaivasal and the great shrine at Sirkazhi.

visit.timings: Typically open only for a short window in the morning, and sometimes again in the early evening; since the priest often keeps limited hours, confirm timings locally before you travel.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirukkurukavur is about 6 km from Sirkazhi, which has the nearest railway station, and about 25 km from both Mayiladuthurai and Chidambaram. On the Sirkazhi to Tirumullaivasal bus route, get down at Vadagal; the temple is about 1 km off the main road. Local transport from Sirkazhi is the easiest way to reach it, and the nearest airport listed is Tiruchirappalli.
